headline: Sheehy, Klobuchar unveil hemp rules bill to replace 11 December ban
dek: The Hemp Guardrails Act, shared on 17 November, would set a 1% total THC limit, a 21+ age floor and FDA oversight, all starting 11 December.
key_points: Sens. Tim Sheehy of Montana and Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota released the Hemp Guardrails Act on 17 November, according to Semafor.
The draft would replace the 0.4 milligram per-container cap due on 11 December with a 1% total THC limit by dry weight and a list of banned intoxicating cannabinoids.
It would make hemp products an FDA-regulated category with a 21+ age limit, US-only supply chains, child-resistant packs and lab results behind a QR code.
The text we read sets no milligram cap per serving or per package, and it has no bill number yet; it still needs a vehicle before the 11 December funding deadline.
body: Two senators from opposite parties have put a full rulebook for hemp THC products on the table, 23 days before most of those products lose federal legality. Sen. Tim Sheehy, a Montana Republican, and Sen. Amy Klobuchar, a Minnesota Democrat, shared the Hemp Guardrails Act with Semafor on 17 November. The draft would scrap the federal restriction that takes effect on 11 December and, on the same day, put hemp-derived cannabinoid products under the Food and Drug Administration.

The bill does three things at once. It rewrites the federal definition of hemp around a 1% total THC limit, it bans a named list of intoxicating converted cannabinoids such as delta-8 THC, and it creates a new chapter of food and drug law for hemp products, with an age floor of 21, US-only sourcing and FDA inspection powers. Semafor reported that Sheehy said the compromise would put bad actors in the hemp market out of business, and that the bill shields farmers, cancer patients and veterans from criminal penalties.
## What the text would change

The draft amends the hemp definition that Congress rewrote in the 2026 agriculture spending law. Where that law uses 0.3%, the bill writes in 1.0%, measured as total THC on a dry-weight basis, including THCA. The sponsors' section-by-section summary says the change is meant to avoid criminalising farm operations, and that the limits due on 11 December would make 95% of consumer hemp products illegal overnight. That 95% figure is the sponsors' claim.

The bill also strikes the clauses behind the 0.4 milligram per-container cap, according to the summary, and replaces them with a ban on more than trace amounts of what it calls restricted cannabinoids. The text defines these as cannabinoids other than delta-9 THC that intoxicate through the CB1 receptor, and names delta-8 THC, delta-10 THC, HHC and THC-O acetate. It expressly leaves out CBD, CBN, CBG, CBC, CBDV, THCV and delta-9 THC itself.

Smokable products get no reprieve. The bill would bar raw hemp flower, smokable flower and pre-rolls sold for inhalation from interstate commerce, a category the sponsors' summary calls gas station weed. Extracts and distillates may run above 1% THC while they are being processed, but only while they stay with permitted manufacturers and never reach a shop shelf.
> The bill swaps a milligram cap for a rulebook, and leaves the strength of a gummy or a drink to the FDA.
## An FDA category, with an age floor

The second half of the bill adds a new Chapter XI to the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act for hemp-derived cannabinoid products. It covers edibles, drinks, tinctures, capsules, inhaled products other than flower, and topicals. Under the text, it would be illegal to sell these products to anyone under 21, for anyone under 21 to possess them, and to ship any product not grown, processed, finished and packaged in the United States. Packaging that imitates images used to market to children would count as misbranding.

Within 180 days the FDA would have to write rules for child-resistant packaging, labels carrying a QR code that links to the product's certificate of analysis, uniform manufacturing and testing standards, third-party testing of finished goods, good manufacturing practice, recalls and facility registration. The agency would gain the power to inspect hemp facilities and seize adulterated or misbranded products. Hemp products would be carved out of the legal definition of tobacco products.

There is also a supplement lane. Non-impairing hemp cannabinoid supplements in forms such as capsules, gummies and tinctures would not be treated as adulterated just because they contain cannabinoids. The text protects a Medicare program, the Substance Access Beneficiary Engagement Incentive, and would let Medicare Advantage plans cover hemp-derived supplements for chronically ill members.
## What the bill leaves out

By our reading of the 17-page text, the bill sets no milligram limit on THC per serving or per package. Delta-9 THC is not on the restricted list, and the only numeric THC test is the 1% dry-weight figure. Any serving-size cap would therefore come, if at all, from the FDA's rulemaking or from states. That matters because per-serving limits were the option the White House floated last year, as we reported on 18 November.

States keep the power to be stricter. The bill says nothing in it limits a state, territory or tribe that wants tougher rules, but it would bar any of them from blocking compliant products passing through on their way elsewhere.
## The politics before 11 December

The bill lands in a Senate already split on hemp. In August the Senate voted 61 to 32 to table an amendment from Sen. Ted Budd of North Carolina that would have stripped the delay from the stopgap bill, The Hill reported, and Budd said then that the fight was just beginning. Semafor reports Budd is preparing another push before the December funding deadline. As we reported on 14 November, Sen. Pete Ricketts of Nebraska has also argued against any further delay.

On the other side, a group of veterans organisations including the VFW sent congressional leaders a letter dated 17 November asking Congress to regulate hemp instead of banning it, with a 21+ age limit, testing, labels and child-resistant packs; Semafor described the coalition as backing the bill. Klobuchar leaves the Senate in January after being elected governor of Minnesota, so the bill also tests whether the deal can outlast one of its two authors.
## What it means for operators

For brands, the draft trades one hard cliff for a long compliance build: US-only sourcing, FDA registration, third-party testing and new packaging within months of enactment. Makers of delta-8 and other converted products would lose their market either way. Flower and pre-roll sellers would lose interstate sales under both the current law and this bill.

The draft carries no bill number, and stand-alone hemp bills have not reached a floor vote this year. The practical path is the funding bill that must pass by 11 December, the same route Rep. James Comer pointed to on 16 November.
## What to watch

Watch for the bill's formal introduction and number, and for Republican co-sponsors beyond Sheehy. Watch whether its language, or any delay, appears in the text of the next funding bill before 11 December. And watch Budd and Ricketts, who could make hemp a condition of their votes on that bill.
